followUps:
It calls persist when the entity is new and merge when it is not, and it decides by asking whether the entity is new. An entity is new if its @Version wrapper field is null, otherwise if a primitive or wrapper id is null (or 0 for primitives), or if it implements Persistable.isNew().

Example: new User() with id null goes to persist (an INSERT). An object with id 7 goes to merge, which runs a SELECT first. That is why assigned ids need Persistable: otherwise every insert costs an extra SELECT.

Hibernate treats it as a new row and inserts it, but only after a SELECT finds nothing. merge loads by id, gets null, then copies your state onto a fresh managed instance and schedules an INSERT.

Example: merging a Product with id 999 that is not in the table gives an INSERT. With a generated id, the new row usually gets a different id from 999, because the generator assigns one; your detached object keeps 999 while the returned copy has the real id. With a @Version field set to a non-null value, Hibernate may instead throw an optimistic locking exception, since it expected an existing row.

code.title: Persistence context: identity map, one SELECT, automatic dirty flush

followUps:
With the default FlushMode AUTO, Hibernate flushes before a transaction commits and before a query whose tables overlap with pending changes, so the query sees them. It also flushes on an explicit flush().

Example: you change order.status, then run select o from Order o where o.status = 'PAID'. Hibernate flushes the UPDATE first so the query returns the right rows. A query on an unrelated table does not have to flush. Native SQL queries flush everything only in some configurations, so call flush() yourself when in doubt.

It tells Hibernate that nothing will be written, so Hibernate skips snapshots and dirty checking, and the flush is skipped. Spring also sets the JDBC connection read-only, which some databases use to route to replicas.

Example: loading 10,000 entities in a read-only transaction saves the snapshot copy of 10,000 objects and the comparison at commit. Changes you make by mistake are silently not saved, so do not use it in methods that write. Cost drops from O(n x properties) at flush to nothing.

code.title: Dirty checking cost: full comparison vs change tracking

followUps:
Because Hibernate only compares by equals, or by reference for some types, a mutable object changed in place may look the same as its snapshot. If the snapshot holds the same object reference, the comparison says nothing changed.

Example: a custom type for a List or JSON object that returns the same instance from deepCopy shows no difference after list.add(x), so no UPDATE runs. Fix it by implementing deepCopy to really copy, flagging the type mutable, and giving it a correct equals. Or use immutable values and replace them instead of editing them.

The benefit is a smaller UPDATE with only the changed columns, the cost is that Hibernate must build the SQL text for every update instead of using one cached statement. Statement caching and JDBC batching also work worse because different updates have different shapes.

Example: on a table with 60 columns where you change 1, the update writes 1 column instead of 60. That helps with wide rows, large text/LOB columns and triggers. On narrow tables it is usually slower overall. Measure before enabling it.

code.title: N+1 query counts: naive lazy loading vs fetch join and batching

followUps:
EAGER only hides the problem and often makes it worse, because the association is now loaded everywhere, even where nobody needs it. Hibernate cannot choose a join per use case.

Example: find by id may join the customer, but a JPQL query from Order ignores the join and runs 50 extra SELECTs for the customers anyway, still 101 queries. Other pages that only need the order id now load customers and items too. Keep associations LAZY and fetch what the screen needs in the query.

Count the SQL statements in a test and fail the build if the number goes up. You assert on the number of statements for a use case, not on speed.

  • Enable Hibernate statistics and assert getPrepareStatementCount().
  • Or use a datasource proxy library that counts queries.
  • Seed realistic data, for example 50 orders, so N+1 shows up as 101 instead of 3.

A test that loads 50 orders and asserts at most 3 statements fails right away when someone removes a fetch join.

code.title: Query counts for lazy, batch fetching, subselect and fetch join

followUps:
Both load the same graph, but fetchgraph treats listed attributes as EAGER and all others as LAZY, while loadgraph treats listed attributes as EAGER and leaves the others at their mapped fetch type.

Example: the entity maps customer as EAGER and items as LAZY. A graph listing only items with fetchgraph makes customer LAZY (and items EAGER). With loadgraph, customer stays EAGER and items becomes EAGER. Use loadgraph when you want to add to the mapping and fetchgraph when you want exact control.

Because Hibernate 6 removes duplicate parent entities from the result of a fetch join automatically, so select o from Order o join fetch o.items returns each order once.

Example: 2 orders with 3 items each give 6 SQL rows. In Hibernate 5, the list had 6 order references (each order three times), so you added distinct. In Hibernate 6 the list has 2 orders. The SQL DISTINCT is also no longer sent for that purpose, which avoids sorting work in the database.

It enables an EntityManager and a database connection for the whole web request, so lazy loading works in the controller and view. Teams disable it because the connection stays held until the response is written, and queries start happening in places you do not see.

Example: a controller that loops over 50 orders and touches order.getItems() triggers 50 lazy queries during JSON writing, with a connection held the whole time. With spring.jpa.open-in-view=false, the same code fails fast with LazyInitializationException and you fix it in the service by fetching what you need.

Do not serialize entities directly. Map them to DTOs inside the transaction and return those, so Jackson only sees plain fields that are already loaded.

  • Records or classes with just the needed fields.
  • Fetch the graph in the service with a fetch join or entity graph.
  • If you must serialize entities, use @JsonIgnore, @JsonManagedReference / @JsonBackReference against cycles, and the Hibernate Jackson module so uninitialised proxies serialize as null.

DTOs also stop you from leaking internal fields.

It uses a soft lock: when a transaction updates an entity, the cache entry is replaced by a lock marker, and the real new value is put back only after the database commit succeeds. While the marker is there, other transactions read from the database instead of the cache.

Example: T1 updates product 5 (marker in cache). T2 reads product 5 mid-update, finds the marker and goes to the database, which returns the old committed row, never a stale cached copy. After T1 commits, the cache holds the new state. The price is a bit more work per write than NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE.

Because Hibernate cannot know which cached rows a bulk or native statement changed, since it does not load the entities. The safe choice is to invalidate the whole region (or all regions for native SQL) so nothing stale is served.

Example: update Product set price = price * 1.1 touches 10,000 rows. Hibernate evicts the entire Product region, so the next reads all hit the database. For native queries you can name the affected entity spaces with addSynchronizedEntityClass to evict only those regions.

code.title: Inner failure marks the shared transaction rollback-only

followUps:
With REQUIRES_NEW the inner method runs in a separate transaction on its own connection, so it commits or rolls back independently and the outer one is not marked rollback-only. With NESTED it uses a savepoint in the same transaction, so a failure rolls back only to the savepoint.

Example: outer saves an order, inner writes an audit row and fails. With REQUIRES_NEW the audit rolls back, the order commits, and the caller catches the exception safely. NESTED gives the same result on one connection, but needs a JDBC driver with savepoints and a JDBC transaction manager (JPA support depends on the dialect).

Because each REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction (which keeps its connection) and takes a second connection. A thread then holds two connections at once.

Example: a pool of 10 connections and 10 threads that each call a REQUIRES_NEW method. All 10 threads hold one connection and wait for a second one that never frees, so the system deadlocks until the pool timeout. Fix it with a pool bigger than the thread count (at least threads x 2), or by avoiding nested new transactions in hot paths.

Move the method to another Spring bean and call it through that bean, because only calls that cross the proxy start a transaction. Calling this.save() bypasses the proxy.

  • Inject another service and call other.save() (best, usually a design improvement).
  • Use TransactionTemplate inside the method.
  • Self-inject the proxy, or use AspectJ mode, which weaves the advice into the class itself.

Example: placeOrder() calling this.audit() with REQUIRES_NEW creates no new transaction; moving audit() to an AuditService does.

It is a helper that runs a block of code in a transaction that you start and end in code, with no proxy involved. It is clearer when only part of a method needs a transaction, or when the same class has to call it.

tx.execute(status -> {
    repo.save(order);
    return null;
});

The transaction commits when the lambda returns and rolls back when it throws or when you call status.setRollbackOnly(). It avoids self-invocation problems and keeps remote calls outside the transaction.

code.title: Optimistic locking with a version column prevents a lost update

followUps:
With DIRTY, Hibernate does not use a version column; it puts only the changed columns in the WHERE clause, comparing them with the values that were loaded. Two users can then change different columns without a conflict.

Example: A changes price, B changes name, both from the same loaded row. UPDATE ... SET price = ? WHERE id = ? AND price = oldPrice succeeds, and B's UPDATE ... WHERE name = oldName also succeeds. It conflicts only if both change the same column. It is Hibernate specific, needs a dynamic update, and is weaker than a version when related fields must stay consistent.

Because the old entity is stale. Retrying with it would fail again with the same old version, or worse, overwrite the other person's change if you copied the new version over it.

Example: A and B both loaded version 3. B's update hits version 4 and fails. The retry must start a new transaction, load the row at version 4, re-apply the change, and save, giving version 5. Also, after a failure the persistence context may be in an unusable state, so a fresh one is needed. Limit retries (for example 3) with backoff.

code.title: Atomic conditional update stops overselling stock

followUps:
The database locks the rows that the SELECT returns from every table in the join, not only the table of your entity, unless you restrict it. That can block unrelated work on joined tables.

Example: select o from Order o join o.customer c ... FOR UPDATE may lock the customer rows too. In PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE OF o locks only the order rows; in JPA with Hibernate use the jakarta.persistence.lock.scope hint or a native query. Fetch only the rows you need, and keep joins out of locking queries when you can.

The database finds a cycle in the wait-for graph (A waits for B, B waits for A), picks a victim and rolls it back. The application sees an exception, for example a PessimisticLockException, or a deadlock error such as SQLState 40001/40P01.

Example: T1 locks row 1 then wants row 2, T2 locks row 2 then wants row 1. After the detector runs (typically within a second or so), one transaction is aborted. Handle it by retrying the whole transaction, and prevent it by locking in a fixed order such as ascending id.

Because Spring Data first loads the entities with a SELECT and then removes them one by one, so it can run lifecycle callbacks and cascades. That is 1 select plus N deletes.

Example: deleteByStatus("OLD") on 10,000 rows runs 1 SELECT and 10,000 DELETE statements, each possibly with child-collection queries. For bulk work, use @Modifying @Query("delete from Order o where o.status = 'OLD'"), which is one statement. It skips callbacks and cascades, and the persistence context must be cleared afterwards.

Page runs an extra COUNT query to know the total number of rows and pages, while Slice only fetches one more row than requested to know whether there is a next page.

Example: page size 20 over 1,000,000 rows. Page issues the select plus select count(*), which can be slow on large tables. Slice runs one select with limit 21 and gives hasNext(). Use Page when the UI shows page numbers and totals, and Slice for infinite scroll or 'load more'.

code.title: Batch size and flush/clear: round trips and managed entities

followUps:
The persistence context keeps every entity and a snapshot of each, so without clearing, memory grows with the row count, and every flush checks all managed entities again.

Example: with 2,000,000 rows and no clear, the 40,000th batch checks about 2 million entities, so the total work grows like n squared over the batch size. With a flush and clear every 50 rows each flush checks 50 entities, so the total is about 2 million checks. The same change prevents OutOfMemoryError.

Make each chunk independent and record progress, so a restart continues after the last committed chunk rather than from row 1.

  1. Commit each batch in its own transaction (for example 1,000 rows).
  2. Save the last processed id or file offset in the same transaction.
  3. Make inserts idempotent (unique key, or upsert) so a replayed chunk does no harm.

Example: it fails at row 1,200,000; the progress record says 1,199,000, so it resumes there. Spring Batch provides this with job repositories and chunk-oriented steps.
